files.lesson.md: --- order: 20 unit: quad9 node: AC9M9A04 n3 uses: [AC9M9A04 n2, AC9M9A01 n3] assumes: [AC9M9A04 n2, AC9M9A01 n3] connection: garden-area title: Solving by factorising summary: "If two numbers multiply to give 0, one of them must be 0. That turns a factorised quadratic into two simple equations." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A garden bed is x m wide and 3 m longer than it is wide, and it must cover 40 square metres. How wide is it?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8367 url: http://127.0.0.1:8367/index.html readySelector: "#board" layout: full --- A quadratic equation often has two solutions. Factorising finds both, and then the situation decides which one makes sense. ## Predict: how wide? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a width for a garden of 40 square metres shows who tries numbers and who sets up an equation. Many will guess 5 or 6." check: type: predict q: "A garden bed is $x$ m wide and $(x + 3)$ m long, with an area of 40 square metres. How wide is it?" options: - "5 m" - "4 m" - "6 m" - "7 m" actual: "5 m. Check: 5 × (5 + 3) = 5 × 8 = 40. The equation x(x + 3) = 40 also has a second solution, x = −8, but a width can't be negative." ``` Try some widths. Which one gives an area of 40? ## Run: where the curve meets zero ```step stage: run insight: "Plotting x(x + 3) − 40 shows the solutions as the x-intercepts: there are two, and only one is a width." try: { playground: board, starter: "solve.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag $P$ to the right-hand place where the curve meets the $x$-axis. Was your prediction right?", when: "x(P) = 5 and y(P) = 0" } ``` The curve is $y = x(x + 3) - 40$: the area minus 40. Where it's 0, the area is exactly 40. ## Investigate: the null factor law ```step stage: investigate insight: "If a product is 0, one of the factors must be 0. So (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0 gives x + 8 = 0 or x − 5 = 0, and the solutions are the opposite signs of the numbers in the brackets." tasks: - check: type: question q: "$(x + 8)(x - 5) = 0$. What are the solutions?" options: ["$x = -8$ or $x = 5$", "$x = 8$ or $x = -5$", "$x = 8$ or $x = 5$", "$x = -3$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Check: if x = 8, x + 8 = 16 and x − 5 = 3, so the product isn't 0.", "If x = 8, x + 8 = 16, not 0.", "That adds the brackets' numbers. Each bracket gives its own solution."] explain: "x + 8 = 0 gives x = −8, and x − 5 = 0 gives x = 5." - check: type: number q: "Solve $x^2 - 7x + 12 = 0$. What is the smaller solution?" answer: 3 explain: "(x − 3)(x − 4) = 0, so x = 3 or x = 4. The smaller is 3." smaller: check: { type: "question", q: "Two numbers multiply to 12 and add to $-7$. Which pair?", options: ["−3 and −4", "3 and 4", "−2 and −6", "−1 and −12"], answer: 0, explain: "−3 × −4 = 12 and −3 + −4 = −7." } - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#alex" text: "Alex solves a quadratic. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: factor-solution-sign explain: "Line 3: x − 2 = 0 gives x = 2, not −2. The solutions are the numbers that make each bracket 0: x = 2 or x = 3." - check: type: number q: "Solve $x^2 - 9x + 14 = 0$. What is the larger solution?" answer: 7 explain: "(x − 2)(x − 7) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 7." ``` ### The null factor law Here's solving the garden equation. ```worked x(x + 3) = 40 :: The garden: width times length is the area. x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0 :: Expand and make one side 0. (x + 8)(x - 5) = 0 :: Factorise: 8 × −5 = −40 and 8 + (−5) = 3. x + 8 = 0 \text{ or } x - 5 = 0 :: If a product is 0, a factor is 0. x = -8 \text{ or } x = 5 :: Both solve the equation. x = 5 \text{ (a width can't be negative)} :: The situation picks one. ``` Now try one on paper: $x^2 + x - 12 = 0$. Factorise, find both solutions, then type the positive one. ### Smaller solution ### Find the mistake Read Alex's working. Which line gets a sign wrong? ### Larger solution ## Modify: change the equation ```step stage: modify insight: "Matching the factors to the x-intercepts: the solutions are where the curve crosses, and some equations have only one." try: { playground: board, starter: "solve.yml#vary", height: 560 } tasks: - hint: ["The curve crosses where each bracket is 0.", "x − p = 0 gives x = p."] check: { type: board, text: "Set $p$ and $q$ so that $(x - p)(x - q) = 0$ has the solutions $2$ and $6$.", when: "p + q = 8 and p * q = 12" } - hint: ["Write x(x + 2) = 24 as x² + 2x − 24 = 0.", "Which two numbers multiply to −24 and add to 2?"] check: { type: number, q: "A rectangle is $x$ m wide and $(x + 2)$ m long, with area 24 square metres. How wide is it?", answer: 4, explain: "x² + 2x − 24 = 0, so (x + 6)(x − 4) = 0. x = −6 or x = 4. A width can't be negative, so x = 4." } - hint: ["Set p and q to the same number on the board.", "How many places does the curve touch the axis?"] check: { type: question, q: "Edge case: $x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0$ factorises as $(x - 3)(x - 3) = 0$. How many solutions does it have?", options: ["One: x = 3", "Two: x = 3 and x = −3", "None", "Three"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "Both brackets give x = 3, so −3 isn't a solution.", "x = 3 works: 9 − 18 + 9 = 0.", "A quadratic never has three."], explain: "Both brackets give x = 3. The curve touches the x-axis at one point: x = 3." } ``` ### Solutions 2 and 6 ### Another garden ### One solution ## Practise: solve and decide ```step stage: practise insight: "Factorise, solve, and then use the situation to pick: the answer to the equation is not always the answer to the problem." tasks: - check: type: number q: "Solve $x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0$. What is the larger solution?" answer: -2 explain: "(x + 2)(x + 3) = 0, so x = −2 or x = −3. The larger one is −2." - check: type: number q: "Solve $x^2 - 3x - 10 = 0$. What is the positive solution?" answer: 5 explain: "(x − 5)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 5 or x = −2." smaller: check: { type: "question", q: "Two numbers multiply to $-10$ and add to $-3$. Which pair?", options: ["−5 and 2", "5 and −2", "−5 and −2", "−10 and 1"], answer: 0, explain: "−5 × 2 = −10 and −5 + 2 = −3." } - check: type: question q: "A rectangle is $x$ m wide and $(x + 4)$ m long with area 32 m². The equation gives $x = 4$ or $x = -8$. Which is the width?" options: ["4 m: a width can't be negative", "−8 m: it's the smaller solution", "Both: they both solve the equation", "Neither"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A length can't be negative.", "Both solve the equation, but only one makes sense as a width.", "4 × (4 + 4) = 32, so 4 works."] explain: "Both numbers solve x² + 4x − 32 = 0, but only x = 4 can be a width." - check: type: number q: "Review: a parabola crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 2$ and $x = 8$. What is the $x$-coordinate of its turning point?" answer: 5 explain: "(2 + 8) ÷ 2 = 5." ``` ### Larger solution ### Positive solution ### Which is the width? ### Review From the last lesson: the axis is halfway. ## Make: the garden bed ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the garden: solve the equation, then say which solution answers the question and why." tasks: - hint: ["Expand and move the 40 across.", "Then factorise."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "The bed is $x$ m wide and $(x + 3)$ m long, with area 40 m². Solve $x(x + 3) = 40$ and type the width in metres." steps: - ["$x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0$", "expand and make one side 0"] - ["$(x + 8)(x - 5) = 0$", "8 × −5 = −40 and 8 + (−5) = 3"] - ["$x = -8 \\text{ or } x = 5$", "each bracket gives a solution"] - ["$x = 5$", "a width can't be negative"] answer: "5" answerLabel: "Width (m)" tolerance: 0.001 feedback: - ["-8", "That solves the equation but a width can't be negative."] - ["8", "8 is the length (x + 3 = 8). The width is x."] criteria: - "I made one side 0 before factorising." - "I found both solutions." - "I used the situation to choose the width." explain: "x = −8 or 5. A width can't be negative, so x = 5 m (and the length is 8 m)." - check: type: question q: "Why do we reject $x = -8$?" options: ["A length can't be negative", "It's too big", "It doesn't solve the equation", "It's the smaller solution"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "It's the wrong sign, not the wrong size.", "(−8 + 8)(−8 − 5) = 0, so it does solve the equation.", "Being smaller isn't the reason."] explain: "x = −8 solves the equation but gives a negative width, which doesn't exist." ``` ### The width Back to the garden. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### Why reject −8? The bed and its area here are made up for the task. **Also used in** - **Design and building.** Rooms, paving and signs are often sized by area equations like this. - **Science.** Equations for a ball's flight or a car's braking can be solved by factorising when they have whole-number solutions. - **Next lesson.** Solving the same equation three ways: algebra, a graph and a table. ```teacher summary: Students solve a monic quadratic equation by factorising and the null factor law, and use the situation to choose a sensible solution (AC9M9A04, node 3). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 14 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 15 min goals: - I can use 'if a product is 0, a factor is 0' to solve a factorised equation. - I can make one side 0, factorise and find both solutions. - I can say which solution fits the situation, and why. struggle: "The sign of the solution: x − 2 = 0 gives x = 2. Ask: what number makes this bracket 0?" before: > Students need Factorising quadratics and Graphing a quadratic. The one idea: if two things multiply to 0, one of them is 0. The common mistake is writing the number in the bracket as the solution without changing its sign (Alex's working). The garden's size is made up for the task. In a real design, a hedge or a fence would take space too. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose 6 or 7 tried numbers: ask them to check the area." - "Run: ask students to find the second place where the curve meets the axis, and say what it would mean for the garden." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the garden in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for 'make one side 0' written first." - "Modify: before the board task, ask which number each bracket needs to be 0." stuck: - see: A student answers x = −2 for (x − 2) = 0. ask: What is −2 − 2? fix: −4, not 0. x = 2 makes the bracket 0. - see: A student solves x(x + 3) = 40 by saying x = 40 or x + 3 = 40. ask: Does the null factor law work when the product is 40? fix: "Only when it's 0: move the 40 over first." stretch: Make up a rectangle problem whose equation has the solutions 3 and −7. support: A list of factor pairs of the constant, with their sums, to choose from. leads: > Continues AC9M9A04 node 3. Where it leads: three ways to solve the same quadratic (next), then modelling stopping distances. exit: q: Solve x² − 4x − 5 = 0. a: (x − 5)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 5 or x = −1. explain: > If two numbers multiply to give 0, one of them must be 0. So (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0 means x + 8 = 0 or x − 5 = 0. Move everything to one side, factorise, solve each bracket, and then decide which solutions make sense in the situation. ```

# region: run
widget: graph

y: -45, 25
grid: 1, 5
snap: 1

point P: 0, 0, drag

widget: graph

y: -12, 20
